requirements.quote:
For all parts of the DNS that are part of the official protocol, all
comparisons between character strings (e.g., labels, domain names, etc.)
are done in a case-insensitive manner.  At present, this rule is in
force throughout the domain system without exception.
requirements.condition: For character-string comparisons in all parts of the official DNS protocol.
requirements.required_behavior: Perform comparisons of character strings, including labels and domain names, in a case-insensitive manner.
requirements.why_checkable: Comparison routines and mixed-case labels or names can be inspected and tested for equal treatment.

requirements.quote:
However, future
additions beyond current usage may need to use the full binary octet
capabilities in names, so attempts to store domain names in 7-bit ASCII
or use of special bytes to terminate labels, etc., should be avoided.
requirements.condition: When choosing the internal representation of domain names, allowing for future use of full binary octets.
requirements.forbidden_behavior: Domain-name storage restricted to 7-bit ASCII should be avoided.
requirements.why_checkable: The representation and conversion paths can be inspected for loss of the high bit; this is advisory guidance.

requirements.quote:
However, future
additions beyond current usage may need to use the full binary octet
capabilities in names, so attempts to store domain names in 7-bit ASCII
or use of special bytes to terminate labels, etc., should be avoided.
requirements.condition: When choosing the internal representation of labels, allowing for future use of full binary octets.
requirements.forbidden_behavior: Use of special bytes to terminate labels should be avoided.
requirements.why_checkable: Label representations can be inspected for reserved terminator bytes that prevent preserving arbitrary label octets; this is advisory guidance.

requirements.quote:
When data enters the domain system, its original case should be
preserved whenever possible.
requirements.condition: When data enters the domain system and preserving its original case is possible.
requirements.required_behavior: The original character case of incoming data should be preserved.
requirements.why_checkable: Insertion and retrieval can compare input and stored character case where no structural name collision requires a shared spelling.

requirements.quote:
The basic rule is that
case can be discarded only when data is used to define structure in a
database, and two names are identical when compared in a case
insensitive manner.
requirements.forbidden_behavior: Discard case when the data is not being used to define database structure.
requirements.why_checkable: Case-folding or canonicalization paths can be checked to ensure that only structural database data loses case.

requirements.quote:
The basic rule is that
case can be discarded only when data is used to define structure in a
database, and two names are identical when compared in a case
insensitive manner.
requirements.condition: When discarding character-case information while using data to define database structure.
requirements.forbidden_behavior: Discard case unless the two names are identical under a case-insensitive comparison.
requirements.why_checkable: Database merging paths can be checked for a case-insensitive identity guard before case information is discarded.

requirements.quote:
For example, if two RRs are stored in a database, one at x.y and
one at X.Y, they are actually stored at the same place in the database,
and hence only one casing would be preserved.
requirements.condition: When storing two resource records whose owner names differ only in character case.
requirements.required_behavior: Treat the case-equivalent owner names as the same database location.
requirements.why_checkable: Inserting records under two case variants of one owner name can verify that the variants share database name identity.

requirements.quote:
Thus while data for x.y
and X.Y may both be stored under a single location x.y or X.Y,
requirements.condition: When storing data under two names that are identical except for character case, such as x.y and X.Y.
requirements.required_behavior: The database may store both names at a single location retaining either of their original casings.
requirements.why_checkable: A database that coalesces case-equivalent names can be checked to accept either original spelling as its retained representation.

requirements.quote:
Loss of case sensitive data must be minimized.  Thus while data for x.y
and X.Y may both be stored under a single location x.y or X.Y, data for
a.x and B.X would never be stored under A.x, A.X, b.x, or b.X.  In
general, this preserves the case of the first label of a domain name,
but forces standardization of interior node labels.
requirements.condition: When storing distinct names such as a.x and B.X that share an interior label modulo case but have distinct first labels.
requirements.forbidden_behavior: Change the case of the distinct first labels merely to standardize the shared interior node; a.x and B.X must not become A.x, A.X, b.x, or b.X.
requirements.why_checkable: Insertion and retrieval of names with a shared interior label can verify preservation of the distinct first-label spellings independently of interior-node standardization.

requirements.quote:
Systems administrators who enter data into the domain database should
take care to represent the data they supply to the domain system in a
case-consistent manner if their system is case-sensitive.  The data
distribution system in the domain system will ensure that consistent
representations are preserved.
requirements.condition: When the domain system distributes data supplied with consistent character-case representations.
requirements.required_behavior: Preserve the consistent character-case representations through the data distribution system.
requirements.why_checkable: A consistently cased database can be distributed and the resulting character-case representations compared with the supplied data.
